_comment: Down syndrome in children: the extra chromosome behind the familiar face, taught through dysmorphic features, cardiac screening and family counselling.
name: Down syndrome
subtitle: Features and counselling
oneLine: The extra chromosome behind the familiar face, and the surveillance that changes the outcome

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: An extra chromosome 21, and why the outcome is decided by care

chapters.title: Approach to the child
chapters.blurb: Befriend first, count nothing until the child is calm

chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Age in months, maternal age, and the informant behind the story

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Record age in months for an infant with the informant named, and always record maternal age at delivery as a number. The age frames which milestones are due, the maternal age frames the nondisjunction risk, and both are needed again at counselling.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: When the difference was noticed, and feeds, tone and milestones beside it

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect the complaints in the mother's words and in order: floppy since birth, feeds that take too long, milestones coming late, chest infections again and again. The tempo here is since birth, not days or weeks, which already separates this from any acute illness.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.expect: List each complaint with its own duration and never write the diagnosis as the complaint: write floppy with poor suck since birth and delayed sitting at 8 months, never Down syndrome. Record feeds, infections and stools alongside, since these carry the cardiac and surgical alarms.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Maternal age, antenatal record, development and the family behind the next pregnancy

skill.hx.paed.development.expect: Take all four domains with ages: gross motor, fine motor and vision, hearing and speech, social behaviour. Uneven delay shapes the stimulation plan, and the mother's account is the baseline every review is measured against.

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.expect: Draw three generations for similar features, learning difficulty, early heart disease and marriages within the family. A translocation running in the family rewrites the recurrence risk for every later pregnancy.

skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.expect: Count rooms, earners, distance to the district hospital and who will bring the child for physiotherapy and reviews. Surveillance fails where the plan ignores the journey, the cost and the carer.

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Growth, tone and the face before the heart is touched

skill.gen.paed.appearance.expect: Look for a placid infant with low tone: frog leg posture, head lag, a flat occiput, upslanting eyes with epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, small ears and a tongue that rests forward. Note alertness and response to the mother's face alongside, since interaction is the developmental baseline.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.expect: Record temperature, pulse, respiratory rate and saturation in a calm child, not a crying one. Fast breathing with poor feeding and sweating points to the heart rather than the lungs, and a single reading never decides it.

skill.exam.paed.weight.expect: Weigh naked where possible and plot against the chart: slow weight gain with long feeds and repeated infections warns of cardiac failure behind the poor growth, not poor feeding alone.

skill.exam.paed.length_height.expect: Measure length on a board in an infant and plot it: short length for age with slowing velocity is part of the syndrome, but crossing down across lines with poor weight gain should raise cardiac disease and thyroid failure alongside.

skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.expect: Measure with a non stretchable tape around the occiput and forehead and plot it: a small head follows the syndrome, while a rapidly enlarging fontanelle picture or a coarse changing face with constipation belongs to hypothyroidism instead.

chapters.title: Cardiac examination in the infant
chapters.blurb: Inspection, pulses, murmurs and the failure that decides urgency

skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.expect: Look for breathlessness with chest indrawing, feel where the apex beats and whether it heaves. A hyperdynamic displaced apex with a thrill in a thriving infant still needs an echo, while the same with sweating feeds and poor gain needs it urgently.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.expect: Feel every pulse including the femorals and compare arm and leg pressures where coarctation could hide beside the syndrome. Bounding pulses with a wide pressure point to a large left to right shunt rather than to reassurance.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.expect: Judge the first and second sounds first: a loud pulmonary second sound with a systolic murmur suggests a large shunt with pulmonary hypertension, which is the lesion that cannot wait.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.expect: Characterise the murmur fully: the harsh systolic murmur of an atrioventricular septal defect with its associated signs, or the softer murmur of a ventricular septal defect, each graded with posture and phase. Any murmur here is an echo, never a watch.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.expect: Look actively for failure: fast breathing with basal crackles, an enlarged tender liver, and poor feeding with sweating. Failure with a murmur in this infant moves the child to urgent cardiac review the same day.

stations.title: Examine the infant with suspected Down syndrome
stations.task: This 8 month old boy was noticed floppy at birth with a different looking face, and feeds poorly. Examine his growth, dysmorphic features and tone, and present your findings with a problem list.
examinerQuestions: List the dysmorphic features you found, and name two findings that would favour congenital hypothyroidism instead.
You found generalised hypotonia. How does low tone change what you expect from the milestones and the feeding story?
This infant also has a loud systolic murmur with poor weight gain. What single investigation is urgent, and why?

stations.title: Take a history and counsel the parents
stations.task: The mother of a 2 month old with suspected Down syndrome is waiting with the grandmother. Take a focused history in six minutes, state what confirms the diagnosis, and counsel the family on what the months ahead hold.
examinerQuestions: What single test confirms the diagnosis, and what three types can it show?
The grandmother asks whether the mother's age caused this and whether the next baby will be the same. What do you tell them?
Name three reviews this infant needs in the first year even if he looks well.

skill.down.basics.title: What Down syndrome is
skill.down.basics.oneLine: An extra chromosome 21, common, recognisable, and managed by surveillance
skill.down.basics.why: Students meet the face and stop there, but the face is only the visible part of a multisystem condition whose outcome is decided by the heart, the thyroid, hearing and follow up. Knowing the chromosome story tells you which test confirms it, why maternal age matters, and why a child who looks well still needs an echo.

teach.heading: An extra chromosome, usually from nondisjunction
teach.body:
Down syndrome is the commonest autosomal cause of intellectual disability, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. Most cases arise from failure of the chromosomes to separate in meiosis, so the child carries a full third copy in every cell.

A minority arise differently: by translocation of part of chromosome 21 onto another chromosome, or by mosaicism where only some cells carry the extra copy. The distinction matters because translocation can run in families and changes the counselling for the next pregnancy.

teach.heading: Why maternal age is asked as a number
points: The chance of nondisjunction climbs as maternal age rises, so the mother's age at delivery is the single strongest background risk factor and is recorded as a number.
Advancing age raises the prior probability but never makes the diagnosis: young mothers also have affected babies, and every suspicion still needs a karyotype.
Antenatal screening with nuchal translucency, blood testing and cell free DNA testing estimates this risk before birth, and explains why some babies arrive already suspected.
Where no screening happened, the reason is recorded without blame: late booking, no scan facility nearby, cost, or a decision to continue regardless.

teach.heading: No cure, but a changed trajectory
teach.body:
There is no treatment that removes the extra chromosome, so care centres on early developmental support with physiotherapy, speech and language therapy and occupational therapy, together with scheduled screening for the associated problems.

With modern cardiac surgery and coordinated multidisciplinary care, life expectancy commonly extends into adulthood, and most individuals live with mild to moderate intellectual disability. The outcome depends largely on the heart and on whether the surveillance was done on time.

pitfalls: Calling the diagnosis from the face alone and skipping the karyotype, so translocation and mosaicism are never identified.
Treating young maternal age as excluding the diagnosis, though affected babies are born to mothers of every age.
Telling the family nothing can be done, confusing no cure with no care, when early intervention and screening change the trajectory.

probes.q: What chromosome change causes Down syndrome, and by which commonest mechanism?
probes.a: An extra copy of chromosome 21, most often from failure of chromosomal separation in meiosis, known as nondisjunction.

probes.q: Why does the minority mechanism matter for the family?
probes.a: Because translocation of chromosome 21 material can be inherited from a carrier parent, so parental karyotyping is needed to set the recurrence risk for later pregnancies.

probes.q: If there is no cure, what changes the outcome for a child with Down syndrome?
probes.a: Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy, surgical correction of heart and bowel anomalies, scheduled thyroid, hearing and vision care, and coordinated multidisciplinary follow up.

skill.down.signs.title: The Down picture: tone, face, hands and feet
skill.down.signs.oneLine: Low tone with a recognisable face, plus the hands, feet and head that complete it
skill.down.signs.why: No single feature proves trisomy, but the full set taken together is unmistakable, and students who know only the eyes miss the tone that explains the feeding and the milestones. Reading the whole picture at once is what lets you counsel confidently while the karyotype is pending, and to know which associated problem to chase first.

teach.heading: Tone first, then the face
teach.body:
Hypotonia is the finding that explains the rest: the baby feels floppy to hold, shows head lag on pulling to sit, sucks weakly and takes too long over feeds. It is present from birth and underlies both the feeding story and the slow milestones.

The face follows the familiar pattern: eyes that slant upward with folds at the inner corners, a flat bridge to the nose, small simply formed ears, and a mouth that rests open with the tongue forward. Brushfield spots, pale speckles on the iris, complete the eyes where looked for in good light.

teach.heading: Hands, feet and head complete the picture
points: Hands are short and broad with a single transverse crease across the palm, and the feet show a wide gap between the great toe and the second toe.
The back of the head is flattened with abundant loose skin at the nape of the neck, felt rather than seen.
The palate runs high and arched, and the teeth and speech that follow are delayed alongside the motor milestones.
Growth runs below the curve: short length for age with a small head, which is why every measurement is plotted rather than eyeballed.

teach.heading: What the features do not tell you
teach.body:
Mild or partial features never exclude associated disease: a child with a convincing face still needs an echo, thyroid testing and hearing review, because the heart and the glands do not declare themselves on the face.

Features also never name the chromosome type. Free trisomy, translocation and mosaicism can look alike, so the karyotype is still required even when the picture feels certain, and mosaic children may show softer features with the same surveillance needs.

pitfalls: Naming the syndrome from the eyes alone while never testing tone, so the feeding and milestone story stays unexplained.
Skipping the echo in a child whose face looks mild, though the heart does not follow the face.
Assuming the karyotype adds nothing when the features feel certain, losing the translocation that changes the family counselling.

probes.q: Name four bedside features that together suggest Down syndrome in a newborn.
probes.a: Generalised hypotonia with head lag, upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthic folds, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap between the great and second toes.

probes.q: Why is hypotonia examined before the milestones are judged?
probes.a: Because low tone explains weak suck, long feeds, head lag and slow motor milestones together, so milestones read against tone rather than against the calendar alone.

probes.q: The face is typical but the baby feeds well with no murmur. What still must be done, and why?
probes.a: Echocardiography, thyroid testing, hearing and vision review and karyotype confirmation, because associated heart disease, hypothyroidism and sensory deficits do not declare themselves on the face.

skill.down.summary.title: The clinical summary
skill.down.summary.oneLine: Child, tempo, syndrome and systems in one passage
skill.down.summary.why: A Down syndrome summary that lists the face and stops leaves the consultant asking about growth, heart, development and karyotype before any plan can be made. Stating the tempo as since birth with the systems in order is what turns a list of features into a case.

teach.heading: What the summary must carry
points: Name the child with age in months, sex, informant and maternal age at delivery, since age frames the milestones and maternal age frames the cause.
State the tempo: features and low tone noticed since birth, with feeding, infections, stools and milestones in the mother's words.
State the syndrome abstractly: the dysmorphic features with generalised hypotonia, growth position on the chart, and developmental level across domains.
Close with the systems: murmur characterised with failure state, thyroid and hearing position, karyotype status with type, and the problem list that hands to the plan.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
An 8 month old boy, second child of a 38 year old mother, noticed floppy at birth with the typical face, now sitting with support with slow weight gain and two chest infections. Examination shows growth below the curve, upslanting eyes with epicanthic folds, a single palmar crease, a sandal gap, generalised hypotonia and a loud systolic murmur with mild liver enlargement.

This is Down syndrome with a complete atrioventricular septal defect and failure to thrive, karyotype awaited, and the child needs early intervention, urgent cardiac review, thyroid and hearing screening, and parental counselling.

pitfalls: Summarising the face without growth, tone, heart and karyotype status, so the listener cannot judge urgency.
Describing a since birth condition with an acute tempo out of habit, which buries the developmental story.
Omitting the negatives, such as no bilious vomiting or bleeding, which are doing real work to exclude surgical and blood alarms.

probes.q: What element belongs in a Down syndrome summary that a general paediatric summary would not usually carry?
probes.a: Maternal age at delivery with the karyotype status and type, because they name the mechanism and set the recurrence counselling no plan can skip.

probes.q: Why does the cardiac state close the summary instead of opening it?
probes.a: Because the listener first needs the child, the tempo and the syndrome to judge the murmur, and the failure state then hands directly to the urgency of the plan.

rubric.text: States age, informant and maternal age with the presenting story
Includes growth, development, cardiac state and karyotype status

skill.down.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.down.differential.oneLine: Slow floppy babies who are not trisomy, and heart defects without the syndrome
skill.down.differential.why: Most slow floppy babies do not have Down syndrome, and most heart defects occur without any syndrome at all. The differential protects both flanks: missing congenital hypothyroidism costs a treatable cause of delay, while calling every dysmorphic baby trisomy without a karyotype chains the family to a wrong recurrence risk.

teach.heading: A slow floppy baby who is not trisomy
points: Congenital hypothyroidism overlaps most closely: hypotonia with coarse features, prolonged jaundice, constipation, a large fontanelle and an umbilical hernia favour the thyroid, and a single blood test both proves it and starts the cure.
Other trisomies, 18 and 13, share low tone and dysmorphism but run a far more severe course with early cardiac and neurological collapse, and are distinguished by karyotype rather than by impression.
Zellweger spectrum and other syndromes with hypotonia bring their own organ patterns, such as liver and bone involvement, without the characteristic face, hands and feet of trisomy 21.

Other syndromic causes of intellectual disability, such as fragile X, Turner and Noonan syndromes, each carry their own feature sets and growth patterns, and the karyotype with clinical correlation separates them.

teach.heading: A heart defect without the syndrome
teach.body:
Ventricular and atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot and coarctation all occur alone in children without any syndrome. The murmur and the failure are worked up identically, and it is the face, tone, hands and growth together that add the syndrome, never the murmur by itself.

An innocent murmur with a thriving child, normal tone and no dysmorphism belongs to neither list. Labelling it syndromic without features, or missing a real defect because the face distracted from the chest, are the two errors this differential exists to stop.

pitfalls: Treating hypothyroidism as excluded by the face, though the two coexist and the thyroid test is cheap and curative.
Calling other trisomies excluded because the baby looks well today, when only the karyotype distinguishes them.
Working up the murmur and forgetting the syndrome, or naming the syndrome and forgetting the echo.

probes.q: A floppy infant has the Down face but also prolonged jaundice, constipation and a large fontanelle. What must be tested, and why?
probes.a: Thyroid function for congenital hypothyroidism, because it overlaps in tone and features, coexists with trisomy, and is treatable where trisomy itself is not.

probes.q: How do trisomy 18 and 13 differ from trisomy 21 in the differential, and what test settles it?
probes.a: They share low tone and dysmorphism but run a far more severe early course, and clinical impression never settles it: karyotype distinguishes the three.

rubric.text: Separates hypothyroidism, other trisomies and other syndromes from trisomy 21
Separates isolated cardiac defects and innocent murmurs from syndromic disease

skill.ix.down.workup.title: Working up suspected Down syndrome
skill.ix.down.workup.oneLine: Confirm with karyotype, then screen the heart, thyroid, blood, ears and eyes
skill.ix.down.workup.why: Tests in Down syndrome do two separate jobs, confirming the chromosome and finding the associated problems that decide management, and ordering them as one undifferentiated panel wastes the family's money while missing the schedule that makes surveillance work. The karyotype comes first because everything else, including the counselling, depends on its type.

teach.heading: Confirm with karyotype first
points: Karyotype confirms trisomy 21 and names the type: free trisomy from nondisjunction, translocation, or mosaicism, which decides the counselling.
Where translocation is found, karyotype both parents to find a carrier, since a carrier parent rewrites the recurrence risk for every later pregnancy.
Antenatal cell free DNA testing and invasive testing belong to pregnancy, not to the born child: after birth the karyotype on the child is the test.
A normal karyotype in a convincing face should prompt review for mosaicism and for the mimics, not quiet acceptance of either result alone.

teach.heading: Heart, thyroid and blood on schedule
points: Echocardiography in every child at diagnosis looks for atrioventricular septal defect and other congenital heart disease, since the heart cannot be cleared by listening alone.
Thyroid function testing at birth and on a scheduled basis finds hypothyroidism that mimics and worsens developmental delay, and treatment is replacement once found.
Full blood count screens the newborn for transient myeloproliferative disorder and later childhood for leukaemia, so pallor, bruising or abnormal counts are never watched.
Cervical spine assessment is reserved for symptoms of cord compression from atlantoaxial instability, not done as routine imaging.

teach.heading: Ears, eyes, growth and sleep
teach.body:
Hearing and vision are assessed on schedule from infancy, since uncorrected deficits silently compound the developmental delay. Growth is plotted at every visit against the chart, because crossing down across lines points to the heart or thyroid rather than to the syndrome alone.

Ask about sleep at every review: noisy breathing with pauses, mouth breathing and daytime inattention warn of obstructive sleep apnoea, which is common, testable and treatable. Where no echo, thyroid test or hearing review is at hand, the child is referred upward rather than labelled screened.

pitfalls: Clearing the heart by stethoscope and skipping the echo, though assuming a normal heart without imaging is the classic error.
Testing thyroid once and never again, so acquired hypothyroidism declares itself as lost milestones years later.
Sending a battery of scans while the karyotype is still pending, answering nothing until the type is known.

probes.q: What single test confirms Down syndrome, and what three types can it show?
probes.a: Karyotype, showing free trisomy 21 from nondisjunction, translocation of chromosome 21 material, or mosaicism.

probes.q: The newborn screen is done and the baby looks well with no murmur. Which two tests must still happen now?
probes.a: Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease that listening cannot exclude, and thyroid function testing at birth with scheduled repeats.

probes.q: A 4 year old with Down syndrome snores loudly with pauses and is inattentive by day. What is suspected and what is the next step?
probes.a: Obstructive sleep apnoea, common in this group, needing sleep review and assessment rather than dismissal as ordinary snoring.

skill.down.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis: karyotype names it, the type shapes the counselling
skill.down.diagnosis.oneLine: Clinical suspicion plus karyotype, stated with type and problem list
skill.down.diagnosis.why: A diagnosis of Down syndrome without the karyotype type is half a diagnosis: it names the child but cannot counsel the parents about the next pregnancy. Stating the features, the type, and the associated problems found or still open is what turns suspicion into a diagnosis the family can use.

teach.heading: Suspicion plus karyotype
teach.body:
The diagnosis is assembled from the clinical picture, generalised hypotonia with the characteristic face, hands and feet, together with karyotype confirmation of trisomy 21. Neither half stands alone: features without karyotype leave translocation unknown, and a laboratory result without the examined child leaves the associated problems unmapped.

A complete statement names the syndrome, the chromosome type, and the problem list: heart, thyroid, hearing, vision, growth, development and blood, each marked done, abnormal, or pending.

teach.heading: Three types, three counselling paths
points: Free trisomy from nondisjunction is the commonest type, tied to advancing maternal age, with the standard age related recurrence discussion for the next pregnancy.
Translocation needs parental karyotyping: a carrier parent carries a substantially higher recurrence risk, and the wider family may need testing too.
Mosaicism means only some cells carry the extra chromosome, features may be softer, and the child keeps the same surveillance needs while the family is counselled on the milder range.
Every type needs the same associated problem screen: the type changes the counselling, never the surveillance.

teach.heading: Antenatal diagnosis and the Indian route
teach.body:
Where antenatal screening or invasive testing has already suggested trisomy, the postnatal karyotype still confirms and types it, and the delivery is planned where the newborn heart review can happen. Where no screening happened, the postnatal pathway starts from the features and catches the screening up.

District hospitals link upward for karyotype and echo through early intervention centres and medical college genetics clinics, and the diagnosis is recorded with the type so no later doctor repeats the search.

pitfalls: Stating Down syndrome without the karyotype type, leaving the recurrence question unanswerable.
Reassuring the family on the heart from a normal examination while the echo is still pending.
Recording the diagnosis without the problem list, so thyroid, hearing and blood fall through the cracks.

probes.q: What two halves make the complete diagnosis of Down syndrome?
probes.a: The clinical picture of hypotonia with the characteristic features, together with karyotype confirmation naming free trisomy, translocation or mosaicism.

probes.q: The karyotype shows translocation trisomy. What must happen next, and why?
probes.a: Karyotype both parents to find a carrier, because a translocation carrier faces a substantially higher recurrence risk that rewrites counselling for every later pregnancy.

probes.q: Why does mosaicism not reduce the surveillance even if features look mild?
probes.a: Because associated heart disease, hypothyroidism, sensory deficits and leukaemia risk follow the diagnosis whatever the proportion of affected cells, so the screen stays complete.

rubric.text: States both the clinical picture and the karyotype with its type
Lists associated problems as done, abnormal or pending
Links the type to parental testing and recurrence risk

skill.tx.down.care.title: Caring for the child with Down syndrome
skill.tx.down.care.oneLine: Development first, surgery where needed, hormones replaced, and follow up for life
skill.tx.down.care.why: Students hear no cure and conclude there is no treatment, while the parents hear the diagnosis and ask what happens on Monday. The answer is a layered plan: stimulate development from infancy, repair the heart and bowel where present, replace thyroid hormone, correct hearing and vision, and watch blood and sleep on schedule, all through one coordinating clinic.

teach.heading: Development from infancy, coordinated for life
points: Start early intervention in infancy with physiotherapy for tone and motor milestones, speech and language therapy for feeding and communication, and occupational therapy for daily skills.
Link the family to the district early intervention centre and the paediatric follow up clinic, so reviews, referrals and records live in one place the parents can reach.
Support schooling with realistic goals and protect the child from infection with routine immunisation, since chest infections remain a leading reason for admission.
Plan for adulthood early: most individuals live with mild to moderate intellectual disability and need supported living and work, discussed long before adolescence.

teach.heading: Repair what surgery can repair
points: Refer every significant congenital heart defect, particularly atrioventricular septal defect, to paediatric cardiology after echo, since timing of repair decides survival and lung pressures.
Send bilious vomiting, absent stool or a swollen belly for same day surgical review for duodenal atresia, and refer persistent delayed stool with a tight segment for Hirschsprung workup.
Watch feeding and growth after any repair as closely as before it, because failure to thrive in this group is cardiac, thyroid or feeding related until proven otherwise.
Use the district hospital as the referral route where a cardiac centre is far, and never let distance convert an urgent echo into a routine one.

teach.heading: Hormones, senses, sleep and blood
points: Treat hypothyroidism with replacement therapy once confirmed, and keep testing on schedule afterwards, since acquired failure declares itself as lost milestones.
Correct hearing and vision deficits as found with aids, glasses or surgery, and retest on schedule, since uncorrected senses silently compound the delay.
Ask about sleep at every review and assess noisy breathing with pauses, since obstructive sleep apnoea is common and its treatment restores attention and growth.
Check the blood count in the newborn period for transient myeloproliferative disorder and periodically after, referring pallor, bruising or abnormal counts urgently for leukaemia workup.

teach.heading: Neck, counselling and red flags
points: Assess the neck only when symptoms suggest cord compression from atlantoaxial instability, such as new weakness, clumsiness, neck pain or bladder change, and counsel against high risk neck manoeuvres and contact sports.
Offer genetic counselling with parental karyotyping where translocation is found or suspected, and discuss the recurrence position for the next pregnancy honestly and without blame.
Teach the family the red flags that need same day care: breathlessness with sweating feeds, bilious vomiting, new weakness or neck pain, pallor with bleeding, and pauses in sleep breathing.
Register the child for disability certification and scheme linked support where eligible, so therapy, aids and schooling are funded rather than abandoned.

pitfalls: Hearing no cure and offering no plan, when development, surgery and hormones change the trajectory.
Repairing the heart and discharging the child from surveillance, though thyroid, hearing and blood need lifelong review.
Imaging every neck routinely while missing the symptomatic cord compression that actually needs assessment.

probes.q: There is no cure for Down syndrome. What are the four layers of its care?
probes.a: Early developmental intervention, surgical repair of heart and bowel anomalies, thyroid replacement with hearing and vision correction, and scheduled surveillance of sleep, blood and growth.

probes.q: An infant with Down syndrome feeds with sweating and gains no weight. What does the plan prioritise?
probes.a: Urgent echocardiography with paediatric cardiology referral for congenital heart disease, since failure to thrive with feeding breathlessness is cardiac until proven otherwise.

probes.q: A schoolchild with Down syndrome develops new clumsiness with neck pain after a fall. What is feared, and what is advised?
probes.a: Cervical cord compression from atlantoaxial instability, needing urgent neurological assessment with neck precautions and avoidance of high risk neck manoeuvres and contact sports.

skill.annex.down.surveillance.title: Down syndrome surveillance card
skill.annex.down.surveillance.oneLine: What to check, when, and what follows, on one card
skill.annex.down.surveillance.why: Surveillance fails not from ignorance but from vagueness: everybody knows the thyroid matters, nobody fixed the month it is next tested. This card pins each check to its timing so the child who looks well today still gets the echo, the blood count and the hearing review that decide next year.

teach.heading: Confirm and stage at diagnosis

rows: Names free trisomy, translocation or mosaicism; parents tested where needed
Detects septal defects; cardiology referral with timing of repair
Replacement started where low; repeats catch acquired failure
Finds transient disorder early and leukaemia if counts change

teach.heading: Every review, and the symptom triggered checks
points: Plot weight, length and head circumference at every visit, since crossing down across lines points to the heart or thyroid rather than the syndrome alone.
Review hearing and vision on schedule from infancy, correcting deficits with aids, glasses or surgery, because uncorrected senses compound the delay.
Ask about sleep breathing at every review: snoring with pauses or daytime inattention triggers sleep assessment, not reassurance.
Assess the cervical spine only when neck pain, new weakness, clumsiness or bladder change suggests cord compression, with precautions while awaiting review.
Track development across all four domains at every visit and adjust physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy to the slowest domain.

pitfalls: Testing thyroid once and calling surveillance done, though acquired failure arrives years later.
Clearing hearing by clapping in clinic instead of scheduled audiology, missing the deficit that slows speech.
Screening the neck routinely while the symptomatic child waits, inverting the only indication imaging has.

probes.q: Which four checks belong to the diagnosis visit itself?
probes.a: Karyotype for type, echocardiography for heart disease, thyroid function at birth, and a newborn blood count for transient myeloproliferative disorder.

probes.q: Why is growth plotted at every review rather than once?
probes.a: Because crossing down across the lines warns of cardiac failure or acquired hypothyroidism behind the poor gain, not of the syndrome alone.

cases.title: A floppy infant with slow gain and repeated chest infections
cases.opening: Priya Jadhav carries in her 8 month old son Aarav, who feels heavy and floppy in her arms. She says he feeds slowly, gains little, and has needed a doctor twice for chest infections. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Aarav Jadhav
patient.residence: Rural village near Ahmednagar, lives with parents, elder sister and grandmother

cues: why have you come to hospital
how can I help your son
presenting.reply: Doctor, since birth Aarav feels loose and floppy, he feeds very slowly and gains little weight. Twice he had fast breathing with fever and needed medicines.

first_noticed.reply: The nurse said at birth itself that his face looks different and his body is very loose. His face has looked the same since then, but the floppiness worries me more now that he should sit.

feeding_account.reply: Breastfeeds with top milk, but each feed takes nearly an hour and he tires and sweats on the breast. Sometimes milk comes out through the nose. Weight gain is very slow.

cues: how does he feel to hold
floppiness.reply: He feels heavy and slips through my hands when I hold him upright. His head still wobbles without support. His cry is soft, not like his sister's cry at this age.

milestone_record.reply: Smiled at nearly four months, babbles a little now, sits only when I prop him with pillows. He reaches for objects but drops them quickly. He recognises me and turns when I call.

chest_infections.reply: Twice he had fast breathing with fever and cough, treated with syrups at the rural hospital without admission. During feeds his lips sometimes look dusky, then become pink again.

stool_belly.reply: He passed the first stool a day after birth, and now passes stool every two or three days, hard. No green vomiting, and the belly is soft without swelling.

sleep_snore.reply: He snores softly with his mouth open but I have not noticed pauses. He sleeps through the night and is alert and playful in the morning.

hearing_vision.reply: He turns when I call and startles to loud sounds. He follows my face with his eyes. No squint that I have seen, and no white reflex.

birth_events.reply: Born at full term in the rural hospital, birth weight two point four kilograms. Cried weakly after birth and sucked poorly for two days, but did not need the newborn unit.

antenatal_record.reply: I booked late at the primary health centre and had one scan near the fifth month, which was reported normal. No special blood tests were done. I took iron and calcium tablets.

past_admissions.reply: No admissions. Mild jaundice for three days needing only sunlight, no fits, no unusual bleeding or bruising. Nobody has mentioned a heart murmur before today.

immunisation_record.reply: Birth vaccines and two rounds done at the anganwadi, card is at home. No reaction. The next round is due this month and I will go.

family_background.reply: Nobody in the family looks like this or has heart disease young. My husband and I married outside the family. My daughter is five and healthy in school.

medicines_given.reply: Only the cough and fever syrups during the infections, and a multivitamin tonic from the shop. No physiotherapy yet, nobody advised it. No allergy we know of.

home_support.reply: My husband works as a farm labourer, we live with his mother who minds Aarav when I work. The rural hospital is six kilometres away, bus costs little. The anganwadi worker visits monthly.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.finding: Placid infant lying with frog leg posture, low tone throughout. Flat occiput with abundant neck skin, upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge, small ears, tongue resting forward. Alert, follows mother face.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.finding: Temperature 37.1 C. Pulse 148 regular, all peripheral pulses felt including femorals. Respiratory rate 42 with mild subcostal indrawing. SpO2 95 percent on room air. Blood pressure 84/52 in the right arm.

skill.exam.paed.weight.finding: Weight 6.2 kg, plotted below the expected curve for an 8 month old boy, with slowed velocity since 4 months. Length and weight both affected, weight more than length.

skill.exam.paed.length_height.finding: Length 64 cm on the board, short for age and plotted below the curve. Upper to lower segment ratio within expected range for age. No limb asymmetry.

skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.finding: Head circumference 41 cm, small for age and plotted below the curve. Anterior fontanelle open and flat, about 2 cm. No coarse changing face, no large fontanelle picture.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.finding: First sound normal, second sound loud over the pulmonary area. No opening snap. No pericardial rub. Basal crackles absent at rest.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.finding: Harsh pansystolic murmur grade 3 best heard at the left lower sternal edge, with a palpable thrill. Murmur unchanged with posture. No ejection click, no continuous machinery quality.

skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.finding: Generalised hypotonia: head lag on pull to sit, slips through the hands on ventral suspension, frog leg posture at rest. Withdraws briskly to touch in all limbs. No asymmetry, no fasciculations.

karyotype.label: Karyotype
karyotype.result: 47 chromosomes with free trisomy 21 in all cells examined. No translocation. No mosaicism.
karyotype.note: This confirms the diagnosis and names the type, which sets the counselling: free trisomy, so no parental carrier testing is needed for this result.

echo.label: Echocardiography
echo.result: Complete atrioventricular septal defect with a large left to right shunt, moderate atrioventricular valve regurgitation, raised pulmonary pressures. Normal arch and no coarctation.
echo.note: This grades the lesion the murmur predicted and decides urgency: a complete defect with failure to thrive needs paediatric cardiology review now, not routine follow up.

tft.label: Thyroid function
tft.result: TSH within the normal range for age with normal free thyroxine. No antibodies tested.
tft.note: Normal today excludes congenital hypothyroidism as a contributor to the delay, but scheduled repeats stay on the card since acquired failure arrives years later.

fbc.label: Full blood count
fbc.result: Haemoglobin, total leucocyte count and platelets within normal range for age. No blasts seen.
fbc.note: Normal counts exclude transient disorder and leukaemia today, while keeping the periodic count on the surveillance card.

bera.label: Hearing assessment
bera.result: Referred for brainstem evoked response audiometry, awaited. Otoacoustic emissions passed on screening.
bera.note: Hearing cannot be cleared by turning to a voice in clinic, so the scheduled audiology test stays pending rather than assumed normal.

vision.label: Eye examination
vision.result: Fixing and following light, no cataract, no nystagmus. Squint assessment with cycloplegic refraction booked.
vision.note: The eye review looks for cataract and refractive error that compound delay, and stays scheduled even with a normal bedside look.

ct_brain.label: CT brain
ct_brain.note: Not indicated: the child is alert with no seizures, no regression and no focal signs, and the delay is explained by tone and the syndrome. Scanning from reflex adds radiation without a question.

torch_panel.label: TORCH titres
torch_panel.note: Not indicated as a first step: there is no microcephaly with calcification, no rash, no jaundice with liver enlargement pattern to suggest congenital infection. It stays on the list only if the karyotype surprises.

differentialModel.answer: Down syndrome with free trisomy 21. Consider congenital hypothyroidism, trisomy 18, trisomy 13, and an isolated atrioventricular septal defect without syndromic features.

diagnosis.answer: Down syndrome with free trisomy 21, with a complete atrioventricular septal defect and failure to thrive.

managementModel.answer: Early intervention with physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy, urgent paediatric cardiology referral for the complete atrioventricular septal defect, scheduled thyroid, hearing and vision review with periodic blood counts, growth monitoring, and genetic counselling for the parents.

teachingPoints: The tempo is since birth, not days or weeks: floppy with the typical face from delivery already separates this from any acute illness before a test is run.
Sweating on feeds with slow gain and dusky lips is the heart speaking, not poor feeding: this history is what makes the echo urgent rather than routine.
Dusky lips during feeds with a loud pulmonary second sound and a thrill at the left edge name a large left to right shunt with pulmonary hypertension, which cannot wait.
A normal thyroid result today excludes congenital hypothyroidism as a contributor but never ends thyroid surveillance, since acquired failure arrives years later.
Hard stools every third day without vomiting or swelling is constipation to manage, not obstruction to operate: bilious vomiting with a swollen belly would be the surgical alarm.
The karyotype type decides the family counselling: free trisomy needs no parental testing, while a translocation result would karyotype both parents.
Two chest infections treated as lung problems alone missed the heart behind them, which is why every infection in this history is rechecked for feeding breathlessness and gain.
